title: Das Hirtenbüblein
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 152. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (fortan, ansehen).
about: KHM 152 is a brief wisdom tale: a shepherd boy's famously sharp answers to hard questions reach the king, who summons him and puts him to a test of three riddling questions — how many drops in the sea, how many stars in the sky, how many seconds in eternity. The boy's answers turn each impossible-sounding question back on its own terms rather than trying to out-compute it, and he is taken into the king's household as a reward. It is short enough to read in one sitting and turns entirely on the cleverness of its three answers.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Hirtenbübchen, das war wegen seiner weisen Antworten, die es auf alle Fragen gab, weit und breit berühmt.
sentences.l: There was once a shepherd-boy, who was, on account of its wise answers that it to all questions gave, far and wide famous.
sentences.i: There was once a shepherd boy who was famous far and wide for the wise answers he gave to every question.
sentences.n: Diminutives in -chen and -lein are neuter, so the boy is “das Hirtenbübchen” and is taken up by “es”, ‘it’, all through the tale; the literal line keeps that. It is grammar, not coldness. “weit und breit” = far and wide.

sentences.t: Der König des Landes hörte auch davon, glaubte es nicht und ließ das Bübchen kommen.
sentences.l: The king of the land heard also of it, believed it not, and let the little-boy come.
sentences.i: The king of that land heard of it too, did not believe it, and had the boy brought before him.
sentences.n: “lassen” with an infinitive means to have a thing done: “ließ das Bübchen kommen” — he had the boy fetched, he did not invite him.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zu ihm „kannst du mir auf drei Fragen, die ich dir vorlegen will, Antwort geben, so will ich dich ansehen wie mein eigen Kind, und du sollst bei mir in meinem königlichen Schloß wohnen.“
sentences.l: Then spoke he to him “can you me to three questions, which I to you put will, answer give, so will I you look upon as my own child, and you shall with me in my royal castle dwell.”
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “If you can give me an answer to three questions that I mean to put to you, I will look on you as my own child, and you shall live with me in my royal castle.”
sentences.n: A conditional built without wenn: the verb stands first (“kannst du…”) and the main clause answers with “so”. “mein eigen Kind” leaves the adjective uninflected, an older usage — the king says it in full, “mein eigenes Kind”, in the last line of the tale.

sentences.t: Sprach das Büblein „wie lauten die drei Fragen?“
sentences.l: Spoke the little-boy “how run the three questions?”
sentences.i: Said the boy, “How do the three questions go?”
sentences.n: “Sprach” at the head of the sentence, with no da or und before it, is the tale-teller’s cadence and returns several times here. “lauten” is used of the wording of a thing — how it runs.

sentences.t: Der König sagte „die erste lautet wie viel Tropfen Wasser sind in dem Weltmeer?“
sentences.l: The king said “the first runs: how many drops of water are in the world-sea?”
sentences.i: The king said, “The first goes: how many drops of water are there in the ocean?”
sentences.n: “das Weltmeer” is the world-sea, the ocean taken as one body. The question is set straight into the sentence with no colon and no quotation marks of its own — the 1857 text often lets speech run on like this.

sentences.t: Das Hirtenbüblein antwortete „Herr König, laßt alle Flüsse auf der Erde verstopfen, damit kein Tröpflein mehr daraus ins Meer lauft, das ich nicht erst gezählt habe, so will ich euch sagen, wie viel Tropfen im Meere sind.“
sentences.l: The shepherd-boy answered “Lord King, have all rivers on the earth stopped up, so that not a little-drop more out of them into the sea runs that I have not first counted, so will I you tell how many drops in the sea are.”
sentences.i: The shepherd boy answered, “My lord King, have all the rivers on earth stopped up, so that not one drop more runs out of them into the sea without my having counted it first, and then I will tell you how many drops there are in the sea.”
sentences.n: The boy addresses the king with “ihr”, the older polite plural — “laßt”, “euch”. “laßt … verstopfen” is again lassen for having a thing done. “lauft” is an older form of läuft. The answer works by hanging the counting on a condition that can never be met.

sentences.t: Sprach der König „die andere Frage lautet wie viel Sterne stehen am Himmel?“
sentences.l: Spoke the king “the other question runs: how many stars stand in the sky?”
sentences.i: Said the king, “The second question goes: how many stars are there in the sky?”
sentences.n: “die andere” means the second of the three — older German uses ander where we now say die zweite. Stars “stand” in the German sky rather than merely being in it.

sentences.t: Das Hirtenbübchen sagte „gebt mir einen großen Bogen weiß Papier,“
sentences.l: The shepherd-boy said “give me a large sheet of white paper,”
sentences.n: “ein Bogen Papier” is a sheet. “weiß Papier” leaves the adjective uninflected, the same older usage as “mein eigen Kind” above.

sentences.t: und dann machte es mit der Feder so viel feine Punkte darauf, daß sie kaum zu sehen und fast gar nicht zu zählen waren und einem die Augen vergiengen, wenn man darauf blickte.
sentences.l: and then made it with the quill so many fine dots on it that they scarcely to be seen and almost not at all to be counted were, and to one the eyes went away when one at it looked.
sentences.i: and then with the quill he made so many fine dots on it that they could scarcely be seen and hardly be counted at all, and one’s eyes swam at the sight of them.
sentences.n: “einem die Augen vergiengen” — the eyes ‘go away’ from a person: an old idiom for sight that fails or blurs. “es” is still the boy. “vergiengen” is the 1857 spelling of vergingen.

sentences.t: Darauf sprach es „so viel Sterne stehen am Himmel, als hier Punkte auf dem Papier zählt sie nur.“
sentences.l: Thereupon spoke it “so many stars stand in the sky as here dots on the paper — count them, do.”
sentences.i: Thereupon he said, “There are as many stars in the sky as there are dots here on the paper — count them, if you will.”
sentences.n: “so viel … als …” is the older comparison where modern German has so viel … wie. “zählt sie nur” is an imperative to the king in the polite plural, and “nur” carries the shrug: go ahead, then.

sentences.t: Aber niemand war dazu im Stand.
sentences.l: But nobody was to it in a position.
sentences.n: “im Stande sein” — to be in a position to do a thing. The 1857 text prints it without the older dative -e on Stand.

sentences.t: Sprach der König „die dritte Frage lautet wie viel Secunden hat die Ewigkeit?“
sentences.l: Spoke the king “the third question runs: how many seconds has eternity?”
sentences.i: Said the king, “The third question goes: how many seconds are there in eternity?”
sentences.n: “Secunden” is the 1857 spelling of Sekunden. In German eternity ‘has’ its seconds, where English asks how many are in it.

sentences.t: Da sagte das Hirtenbüblein „in Hinterpommern liegt der Demantberg, der hat eine Stunde in die Höhe, eine Stunde in die Breite und eine Stunde in die Tiefe;
sentences.l: Then said the shepherd-boy “in Farther Pomerania lies the Diamond-mountain, it has an hour into the height, an hour into the breadth and an hour into the depth;
sentences.i: Then the shepherd boy said, “In Farther Pomerania lies the Diamond Mountain; it is an hour high, an hour broad and an hour deep;
sentences.n: Hinterpommern is Farther Pomerania, the eastern part of the old province — in a tale it means simply somewhere far off. Distance is reckoned in hours of walking, so the mountain measures an hour’s walk each way. “Demant” is the older word for a diamond, modern Diamant.

sentences.t: dahin kommt alle hundert Jahr ein Vögelein und wetzt sein Schnäblein daran,
sentences.l: there comes every hundred year a little-bird and whets its little-beak on it,
sentences.i: every hundred years a little bird comes there and whets its little beak on it,
sentences.n: “alle hundert Jahr” leaves the noun unpluralized after a number, as older German often does. The two diminutives, Vögelein and Schnäblein, set the smallness of the bird against the mountain — that opposition is the whole answer.

sentences.t: und wenn der ganze Berg abgewetzt ist, dann ist die erste Secunde von der Ewigkeit vorbei.“
sentences.l: and when the whole mountain worn away is, then is the first second of eternity past.”
sentences.i: and when the whole mountain has been worn away, then the first second of eternity is over.”
sentences.n: “abwetzen” — to whet away, grind down — is separable. The point is not that eternity is long: after all that, it has not finished its first second.

sentences.t: Sprach der König „du hast die drei Fragen aufgelöst wie ein Weiser und sollst fortan bei mir in meinem königlichen Schlosse wohnen, und ich will dich ansehen wie mein eigenes Kind.“
sentences.l: Spoke the king “you have the three questions resolved like a wise man, and shall from now on with me in my royal castle dwell, and I will you look upon as my own child.”
sentences.i: Said the king, “You have solved the three questions like a wise man, and from now on you shall live with me in my royal castle, and I will look on you as my own child.”
sentences.n: “auflösen” of a riddle is to undo it, to resolve it. The king repeats his opening offer almost word for word, but now with “Schlosse” carrying the older dative -e and “mein eigenes Kind” fully inflected — the boy is being spoken to as one who has earned it.

glossary.ansehen: ansehen — to look upon, to regard as (infinitive; separable)
glossary.bogen: der Bogen — a sheet (of paper); also a bow, an arch
glossary.es: es — it (das Hirtenbübchen is a neuter diminutive, so the boy is “es” all through this tale)
glossary.feder: die Feder — feather; a quill pen
glossary.stand: der Stand — position, standing (im Stande sein: to be in a position to, to be able to)
glossary.tiefe: die Tiefe — depth (noun; also tiefe, the inflected adjective tief, deep)
